<h1 id="Introduction-to-scvi-tools-%E2%80%94-Full-Walkthrough">Introduction to scvi-tools — Full Walkthrough¶</h1><p>A complete, runnable version of the official tutorial: API Overview / Introduction to scvi-tools</p> <p>This notebook walks through the entire scvi-tools workflow. While it focuses on scVI, the API is consistent across all scvi-tools models (scANVI, TotalVI, CELLxGENE, ...).</p> <h2 id="What-you-will-learn">What you will learn¶</h2>
  1. Loading and preparing data — AnnData, raw counts, normalization, highly variable genes
  2. setup_anndata() — registering batches and covariates so the model can correct for them
  3. Creating and training a model — the scikit-learn-style API (SCVI(adata) → model.train())
  4. Saving / loading and reading loss curves (ELBO = reconstruction + KL)
  5. Obtaining model outputs — latent space and denoised/normalized expression
  6. Interoperability with Scanpy — UMAP before/after batch correction, clustering
  7. Differential expression — 1-vs-1 and 1-vs-all tests, marker extraction, plots
  8. Logging verbosity control
<p>Dataset: a subsampled version of the heart cell atlas from Litviňuková et al. (2020), Cells of the adult human heart, Nature 588.</p>
<h2 id="0.-Setup">0. Setup¶</h2><p>T he next cell installs the tutorial dependencies, uncomment the pip install line if you don't have the packages yet.</p>

<hr /> <h2 id="1.-Loading-and-preparing-data">1. Loading and preparing data¶</h2><p>We load a subsampled version of the heart cell atlas dataset. scvi-tools ships many "built-in" datasets and can also load arbitrary .csv, .loom, and .h5ad (AnnData) files.</p>
<p>Important: all scvi-tools models require AnnData objects as input.</p>
In [22]:
adata = scvi.data.heart_cell_atlas_subsampled(save_path=save_dir.name)
adata

<h3 id="1.1-Filter-lowly-expressed-genes">1.1 Filter lowly expressed genes¶</h3><p>Remove genes with very few counts and obvious outliers. For these tasks we prefer Scanpy's preprocessing module (scanpy.pp).</p>
In [23]:
sc.pp.filter_genes(adata, min_counts=3)
<h3 id="1.2-Preserve-raw-counts,-then-normalize-for-visualization">1.2 Preserve raw counts, then normalize for visualization¶</h3><p>In scRNA-seq analysis it is popular to normalize the data. These values are NOT used by scvi-tools — they are kept only for other tasks and for visualization.</p>
<p>Important: unless otherwise specified, scvi-tools models require the raw counts (not log library-size normalized data). Models will run on non-negative real-valued data, but that should only be used when the values genuinely represent pseudocounts (e.g. SoupX-corrected counts), not some other normalized matrix.</p>
<p>So the pattern is:</p>
  1. Copy the raw counts into a layer (adata.layers["counts"])
  2. Normalize + log-transform into .X for Scanpy's downstream steps
  3. Freeze the normalized state in .raw (used by Scanpy plots like use_raw=True)
In [24]:
adata.layers["counts"] = adata.X.copy()  # preserve counts
sc.pp.normalize_total(adata, target_sum=1e4)
sc.pp.log1p(adata)
adata.raw = adata  # freeze the state in `.raw`
<h3 id="1.3-Feature-selection-(highly-variable-genes)">1.3 Feature selection (highly variable genes)¶</h3><p>Feature selection reduces the number of genes used as model input. For scVI, anywhere from 1,000 to 10,000 HVGs is a good range, context-dependent.</p> <p>flavor="seurat_v3" works directly on raw counts (in layer="counts"), and batch_key="cell_source" keeps genes that are variable within batches, not just variable between batches — so we don't select genes that are just batch effects.</p>
In [27]:
sc.pp.highly_variable_genes(
    adata,
    n_top_genes=1200,
    subset=True,
    layer="counts",
    flavor="seurat_v3",
    batch_key="cell_source",
)
<h3 id="1.4-setup_anndata()-%E2%80%94-registering-your-data-with-the-model">1.4 setup_anndata() — registering your data with the model¶</h3><p>This is the step people most often get wrong. setup_anndata() tells scvi-tools where the various matrices live inside the AnnData and which columns should be modeled as covariates.</p> <p>In this dataset:</p>
  • cell_source — categorical covariate (nuclei vs. cells, protocol)
  • within each cell_source: multiple donor, gender, age_group
  • percent_mito, percent_ribo — continuous covariates we want to correct for
<p>If you only have one categorical covariate, use batch_key= instead of categorical_covariate_keys=[...]. Registering a batch means the subsequent model will correct for batch effects.</p>
<p>Warning: if you modify the AnnData after setup_anndata(), you must run it again before creating a model instance.</p>
In [29]:
scvi.model.SCVI.setup_anndata(
    adata,
    layer="counts",
    categorical_covariate_keys=["cell_source", "donor"],
    continuous_covariate_keys=["percent_mito", "percent_ribo"],
)
<hr /> <h2 id="2.-Creating-and-training-a-model">2. Creating and training a model¶</h2><p>The API is inspired by scikit-learn: construct with data, then call .train().</p> <p>scVI in one paragraph: it is a variational autoencoder (VAE) on count data. Each cell is encoded into a low-dimensional latent space, then decoded back to gene counts using a zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) likelihood. Training minimizes the ELBO = reconstruction loss + KL divergence. The latent space is learned such that batch/covariate information is regressed out, giving you a batch-corrected embedding.</p>
In [30]:
model = scvi.model.SCVI(adata)
model

<p>Printing the model shows its hyperparameters:</p>

    

  • n_latent: 10 — dimensionality of the latent space
    • 

  • n_hidden: 128, n_layers: 1 — encoder/decoder size
    • 

  • dispersion: gene, gene_likelihood: zinb — count model
    • 

  • latent_distribution: normal — prior on the latent space
    • 




<p>Note: scvi-tools runs much faster on GPU; it uses one automatically if available.</p>

<h3 id="2.1-Saving-and-loading">2.1 Saving and loading¶</h3><p>Saving stores the network weights plus the parameters needed to re-initialize the model.</p>


















In [32]:






model_dir = os.path.join(save_dir.name, "scvi_model")
model.save(model_dir, overwrite=True)





















In [33]:






model = scvi.model.SCVI.load(model_dir, adata=adata)

























INFO     File /tmp/tmpi40zgwdb/scvi_model/model.pt already downloaded                                              
























<h3 id="2.2-Loss-curves">2.2 Loss curves¶</h3><p>Every scvi-tools model stores its losses in model.history.</p>
<p>How to read them:</p>

<thead>

  <th>Metric</th>
  <th>What it measures</th>

</thead>
<tbody>

</tbody>
<tbody></tbody>

ELBO
The total loss the model optimizes = reconstruction loss + KL divergence (negative ELBO)




Reconstruction loss
How well the original counts are reconstructed/decoded from the latent embedding (the maximum-likelihood term)




KL divergence
Regularization of the latent space — how close the approximate posterior q(z\|x) is to the prior p(z)


<p>Healthy training looks like: train and validation curves decreasing together and converging.</p>

    

  • Overfitting: validation ELBO starts increasing, KL not stable, reconstruction loss on validation explodes
    • 

  • Underfitting: train ELBO has not converged yet
    • 


<p>Both matter for the correctness of downstream analyses.</p>


















In [34]:






import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

hist = model.history


def plot_metric(train_key, val_key, title, ylabel):
    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
    plt.plot(hist[train_key], label="train")
    plt.plot(hist[val_key], label="validation")
    plt.xlabel("Epoch")
    plt.ylabel(ylabel)
    plt.title(title)
    plt.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()





















In [35]:






# Negative ELBO (Evidence Lower Bound) — the total loss
if "elbo_train" in hist:
    plot_metric("elbo_train", "elbo_validation", "ELBO", "ELBO")












































In [36]:






# Reconstruction loss — how well counts are decoded from the latent space
plot_metric(
    "reconstruction_loss_train",
    "reconstruction_loss_validation",
    "Reconstruction loss",
    "Negative log likelihood",
)












































In [37]:






# Local KL divergence — latent space regularization
plot_metric(
    "kl_local_train", "kl_local_validation", "KL divergence (latent z)", "KL(q(z|x)||p(z))"
)

<h2 id="3.-Obtaining-model-outputs">3. Obtaining model outputs¶</h2><p>It is often useful to store model outputs back into the original AnnData — this gives you full interoperability with Scanpy.</p>


















In [41]:






SCVI_LATENT_KEY = "X_scVI"

latent = model.get_latent_representation()
adata.obsm[SCVI_LATENT_KEY] = latent
latent.shape





















Out[41]:




(18641, 10)























<p>model.get_...() functions default to the AnnData used to initialize the model, but you can pass a subset — or even a completely independent AnnData, as long as it is organized the same way.</p>
<p>Two key outputs:</p>

    

  • get_latent_representation() — the learned latent (embedding) space
    • 

  • get_normalized_expression() — the model's denoised gene-space estimates
    • 



















In [44]:






adata_subset = adata[adata.obs.cell_type == "Fibroblast"]
latent_subset = model.get_latent_representation(adata_subset)
latent_subset.shape

In [46]:






SCVI_NORMALIZED_KEY = "scvi_normalized"

adata.layers[SCVI_NORMALIZED_KEY] = model.get_normalized_expression(library_size=10e4)


























<p>Batch correction caveat: to get a full gene-space matrix with batch correction you must use model.get_normalized_expression(..., transform_batch=<reference_batch>). Without transform_batch, the decoded matrix is conditioned on each cell's own batch — so it does not remove batch effects (it is a per-batch decoded expression, not a harmonized one).</p>






















<hr />
<h2 id="4.-Interoperability-with-Scanpy">4. Interoperability with Scanpy¶</h2><p>Scanpy handles visualization and downstream analysis. Here we feed scvi-tools outputs back into a standard Scanpy workflow.</p>
<h3 id="4.1-Visualization-WITHOUT-batch-correction-(PCA)">4.1 Visualization WITHOUT batch correction (PCA)¶</h3>

<p>Warning: UMAP is used only to qualitatively assess embeddings — never quantify with it. The recommended practice is to use scVI's embedding as a drop-in replacement for PCA.</p>


<p>First: PCA + neighbors + UMAP on the raw (log-normalized) data to see the nuisance variation.</p>


















In [47]:






# run PCA then generate UMAP plots
sc.tl.pca(adata)
sc.pp.neighbors(adata, n_pcs=30, n_neighbors=20)
sc.tl.umap(adata, min_dist=0.3)





















In [48]:






sc.pl.umap(
    adata,
    color=["cell_type"],
    frameon=False,
)
sc.pl.umap(
    adata,
    color=["donor", "cell_source"],
    ncols=2,
    frameon=False,
)


























































<p>Cell types are generally well separated, but nuisance variation (donor, nuclei vs. cells) plays a large part in the structure of the data — clusters split by donor rather than biology.</p>
<h3 id="4.2-Visualization-WITH-batch-correction-(scVI-latent-space)">4.2 Visualization WITH batch correction (scVI latent space)¶</h3><p>Now the same plots using the scVI latent space — just tell Scanpy to use it instead of PCA via use_rep=.</p>


















In [50]:






# use scVI latent space for UMAP generation
sc.pp.neighbors(adata, use_rep=SCVI_LATENT_KEY)
sc.tl.umap(adata, min_dist=0.3)





















In [51]:






sc.pl.umap(
    adata,
    color=["cell_type"],
    frameon=False,
)
sc.pl.umap(
    adata,
    color=["donor", "cell_source"],
    ncols=2,
    frameon=False,
)


























































<p>scVI corrects for nuisance variation (nuclei/whole cell, age group, donor) while maintaining separation of cell types — compare with the PCA plots above.</p>
<h3 id="4.3-Clustering-on-the-scVI-latent-space">4.3 Clustering on the scVI latent space¶</h3><p>Neighbors were already computed from X_scVI, so we can cluster directly and, if we want, reinject the clusters into scvi-tools (e.g. for differential expression).</p>


















In [57]:






# neighbors were already computed using scVI
SCVI_CLUSTERS_KEY = "leiden_scVI"
#sc.tl.leiden(adata, key_added=SCVI_CLUSTERS_KEY, resolution=0.5)

sc.tl.leiden(
    adata,
    key_added="leiden_scVI",
    resolution=0.5,
    flavor="igraph",
    n_iterations=2,
    directed=False,
    random_state=42,
)





















In [58]:






sc.pl.umap(
    adata,
    color=[SCVI_CLUSTERS_KEY],
    frameon=False,
)















































<hr />
<h2 id="5.-Differential-expression">5. Differential expression¶</h2><p>Many scvi-tools models provide built-in DE methods. See the API docs for the underlying methods.</p>
<p>Key columns in the result:</p>

    

  • proba_m1 / proba_m2 (or proba_de) — posterior probability that the gene is more expressed in group 1 / group 2
    • 

  • bayes_factor — log-abundance ratio in favor of DE (like a log2FC, Bayesian version)
    • 

  • scale1 / scale2 — model-estimated expression scales
    • 

  • is_de_fdr_0.05 — whether the gene passes FDR correction (in mode="change")
    •

<h3 id="5.3-Extract-top-markers-per-cluster">5.3 Extract top markers per cluster¶</h3><p>Filters applied to each cell type's DE table:</p>

    

  • lfc_mean > 0 — upregulated in that cell type
    • 

  • bayes_factor > 3 — strong evidence for DE
    • 

  • non_zeros_proportion1 > 0.1 — expressed in at least 10% of cells of that type
    • 


<p>Then we keep the top 3 markers each.</p>


















In [63]:






markers = {}
cats = adata.obs.cell_type.cat.categories
for c in cats:
    cid = f"{c} vs Rest"
    cell_type_df = de_df.loc[de_df.comparison == cid]

    cell_type_df = cell_type_df[cell_type_df.lfc_mean > 0]

    cell_type_df = cell_type_df[cell_type_df["bayes_factor"] > 3]
    cell_type_df = cell_type_df[cell_type_df["non_zeros_proportion1"] > 0.1]

    markers[c] = cell_type_df.index.tolist()[:3]





















In [64]:






sc.tl.dendrogram(adata, groupby="cell_type", use_rep="X_scVI")





















In [65]:






sc.pl.dotplot(
    adata,
    markers,
    groupby="cell_type",
    dendrogram=True,
    color_map="Blues",
    swap_axes=True,
    use_raw=True,
    standard_scale="var",
)















































<p>We can also visualize the scVI normalized (denoised) expression values instead of the observed data, using the layer option:</p>


















In [66]:






sc.pl.heatmap(
    adata,
    markers,
    groupby="cell_type",
    layer="scvi_normalized",
    standard_scale="var",
    dendrogram=True,
    figsize=(8, 12),
)

<h2 id="6.-Logging-information">6. Logging information¶</h2><p>Verbosity levels:</p>

<thead>

  <th>Level</th>
  <th>Numeric value</th>
  <th>Shows</th>

</thead>
<tbody>

</tbody>
<tbody></tbody>

CRITICAL
50
almost nothing




ERROR
40
errors only




WARNING
30
a progress bar




INFO
20
global logs, number of jobs done (default)




DEBUG
10
detailed logs for each training step (e.g. parameters tested)




NOTSET
0
everything


<p>Use scvi.settings.verbosity to set the verbosity of the scvi package (values are the standard Python logging levels).</p>


















In [67]:






import logging

# Examples:
# scvi.settings.verbosity = logging.WARNING   # progress bar only
scvi.settings.verbosity = logging.INFO        # default
# scvi.settings.verbosity = logging.DEBUG     # very detailed
























<hr />
<h2 id="Summary-%E2%80%94-the-scvi-tools-API-in-6-lines">Summary — the scvi-tools API in 6 lines¶</h2>
adata = scvi.data.<dataset>()          # 1. load AnnData with raw counts
scvi.model.SCVI.setup_anndata(         # 2. register layers + covariates
    adata, layer="counts", batch_key="..."
)
model = scvi.model.SCVI(adata)         # 3. create model
model.train()                          # 4. train
adata.obsm["X_scVI"] = model.get_latent_representation()   # 5. outputs
model.differential_expression(groupby="cell_type")         # 6. analysis


<p>The same pattern holds for every model in scvi-tools — only the class name and the setup arguments change.</p>
<p>Next steps: see the official tutorial gallery for scANVI (annotation), TotalVI (CITE-seq), MULTIVI (multiome), cellxgene export, and more.</p>
